questions.q: On which date did the Constitution of India come into force?
questions.why: It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, the day India became a republic.

questions.q: Who was elected the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.why: Dr Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary chairman at the first sitting; Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946.

questions.q: Which two words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976)?
questions.why: The 42nd Amendment added ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ (and ‘integrity’) to the Preamble.

questions.q: Why was 26 January chosen as the day for the Constitution to come into force?
o: It was the day the Constituent Assembly first met
On 26 January 1930 Purna Swaraj Day had been celebrated
It was the day the Cabinet Mission arrived
questions.why: After the Lahore Congress resolution of 1929, 26 January 1930 was observed as Purna Swaraj (Independence) Day, so the date was kept to honour it.

questions.q: How were the members of the Constituent Assembly chosen from the provinces in 1946?
o: Indirectly, by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies
questions.why: Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, provincial members were elected indirectly by the provincial assemblies.

long.q: What is meant by a Constitution? State two reasons why a country needs one.
scheme: B1: a Constitution is the basic law of a country: a set of fundamental rules and principles by which it is governed
B1: it sets out the structure, powers and limits of the organs of government (legislature, executive, judiciary)
B1: it protects citizens' rights and places limits on government so power is not misused

long.q: Name the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution. State the dates on which the Constitution was (a) adopted and (b) brought into force.
scheme: B1: Dr B. R. Ambedkar
B1: adopted on 26 November 1949 (celebrated as Constitution Day)
B1: came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day)
long.ans: Dr B. R. Ambedkar; 26 November 1949; 26 January 1950

long.q: The Preamble declares India to be a ‘Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic’. Explain the meaning of any four of these terms.
scheme: B1: Sovereign: India is free to decide its internal and external affairs, with no outside authority over it
B1: Socialist: the state aims to reduce inequality of income and wealth and to ensure social and economic justice
B1: Secular: the state has no official religion and treats all religions equally
B1: Democratic/Republic: power rests with the people who elect their government; the head of state (President) is elected, not hereditary

long.q: Explain what is meant by a ‘welfare state’ and give two ways in which the Indian Constitution aims to make India one.
scheme: B1: a welfare state is one that works for the well-being of all its people, especially the poor and weak, and not only for law and order
B1: the Directive Principles ask the state to secure adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, and public assistance in old age, sickness and unemployment
B1: provision for free and compulsory education, reservation and protection for weaker sections (any one further valid point)

long.q: State any four salient features of the Indian Constitution.
scheme: B1: it is a written and the lengthiest constitution in the world
B1: it sets up a federal system with a strong Centre (a Union of States)
B1: it provides a parliamentary form of government, with the executive responsible to the legislature
B1: any one of: single citizenship; universal adult franchise; Fundamental Rights and Duties; independent judiciary; secular state

topics.name: Salient Features of the Constitution I: Citizenship, Franchise and Fundamental Rights

questions.q: What is the minimum voting age in India under universal adult franchise?
questions.why: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years.

questions.q: Which Fundamental Right did Dr Ambedkar call the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution?
questions.why: Article 32 lets a citizen go directly to the Supreme Court to enforce rights; without it the other rights would be meaningless.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution abolishes untouchability?
questions.why: Article 17, part of the Right to Equality, abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.

questions.q: The Right to Property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by which amendment?
questions.why: The 44th Amendment (1978) made property a legal right under Article 300A instead of a Fundamental Right.

questions.q: Which writ orders a person who has been detained to be produced before a court?
questions.why: Habeas corpus (‘you may have the body’) lets the court check whether a detention is lawful.

long.q: Explain the meaning of single citizenship. How is it different from the arrangement in the USA?
scheme: B1: in India every citizen has only one citizenship, that of India, whichever state he or she lives in
B1: all citizens enjoy the same rights all over the country
B1: in the USA a person is a citizen both of the country and of the state in which he or she lives (dual citizenship)

long.q: What is meant by universal adult franchise? Give two reasons why the framers of the Constitution adopted it.
scheme: B1: every citizen aged 18 or above has the right to vote, without discrimination of caste, religion, sex, wealth or education
B1: it makes the government truly representative of all the people and reflects the principle of political equality
B1: it gives the poor and weaker sections a voice and educates people politically

long.q: Name the six Fundamental Rights now guaranteed by the Constitution.
scheme: B1: Right to Equality; Right to Freedom
B1: Right against Exploitation; Right to Freedom of Religion
B1: Cultural and Educational Rights; Right to Constitutional Remedies

long.q: With reference to the Right to Equality, explain: (a) equality before law, (b) abolition of titles, (c) equality of opportunity in public employment.
scheme: B1: equality before law (Article 14): the state cannot deny any person equality before law or equal protection of the laws; no one is above the law
B1: abolition of titles (Article 18): the state cannot confer titles other than military or academic distinctions, and citizens may not accept foreign titles without the President's consent
B1: equality of opportunity (Article 16): all citizens have equal opportunity in government jobs, though posts may be reserved for backward classes

long.q: State four ways in which the Right against Exploitation and the Right to Freedom protect children and workers.
scheme: B1: Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar)
B1: Article 24 forbids employing children below 14 years in factories, mines or other hazardous work
B1: Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) gives free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14
B1: Article 22 requires an arrested person to be told the grounds of arrest and produced before a magistrate within 24 hours

topics.name: Salient Features of the Constitution II: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties

questions.q: The idea of Directive Principles of State Policy was borrowed from the Constitution of which country?
questions.why: India took the idea of Directive Principles from the Irish Constitution.

questions.q: Which of these is a key difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: Directive Principles cannot be enforced in a court of law
Fundamental Rights apply only to the states
Directive Principles can be suspended only by the Supreme Court
Fundamental Rights were added by an amendment
questions.why: Fundamental Rights are justiciable; Directive Principles are non-justiciable guidelines, though fundamental to governance.

questions.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by which amendment?
questions.why: On the Swaran Singh Committee's advice, the 42nd Amendment added Part IVA (Article 51A) with ten duties.

questions.q: The Directive Principle asking the state to organise village panchayats is an example of which type of principle?
questions.why: Village panchayats, cottage industries and prohibition reflect Gandhiji's ideals of village self-rule.

questions.q: Which Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002?
o: For parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their child aged 6 to 14
questions.why: The 86th Amendment added the eleventh duty, linked to the new right to education.

long.q: What are Directive Principles of State Policy? Why are they said to be ‘fundamental in the governance of the country’?
scheme: B1: they are guidelines in Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36 to 51) for the Central and state governments when they make laws and policies
B1: they aim to establish social and economic democracy and a welfare state
B1: though not enforceable in courts, governments are expected to apply them, and voters can judge governments by them

long.q: State any three Directive Principles that aim at economic and social justice (socialistic principles).
scheme: B1: adequate means of livelihood for all citizens, men and women equally
B1: equal pay for equal work for both men and women
B1: wealth and the means of production should not be concentrated in a few hands / public assistance in old age, sickness and unemployment

long.q: Give two Gandhian principles and two liberal-intellectual principles among the Directive Principles.
scheme: B1: Gandhian: organise village panchayats as units of self-government
B1: Gandhian: promote cottage industries / prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs harmful to health / protect cows and cattle
B1: liberal-intellectual: a uniform civil code for all citizens
B1: liberal-intellectual: separate the judiciary from the executive / protect the environment, forests and wildlife / protect monuments of national importance

long.q: Distinguish between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy on three points.
scheme: B1: Fundamental Rights are justiciable (enforceable in court); Directive Principles are not
B1: Fundamental Rights are mostly negative (they restrain the state); Directive Principles are positive (they direct the state to act)
B1: Fundamental Rights aim at political democracy; Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy

long.q: List any four Fundamental Duties of an Indian citizen.
scheme: B1: to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, the National Flag and the National Anthem
B1: to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
B1: to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife
B1: to safeguard public property and abjure violence / promote harmony and the spirit of brotherhood / develop the scientific temper

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the Election Commission of India?
questions.why: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission.

questions.q: An election held to fill a seat that falls vacant because a member dies or resigns is called a:
questions.why: A by-election (bye-election) fills a single vacancy in a constituency between general elections.

questions.q: Which of these is chosen by an indirect election?
o: A member of the Rajya Sabha
A member of the Lok Sabha
A member of a Legislative Assembly
A member of a Gram Panchayat
questions.why: Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected members of the state legislative assemblies, not by voters directly.

questions.q: Election campaigning must stop how long before polling ends?
questions.why: Campaigning ends 48 hours before the close of polling so that voters can decide calmly.

questions.q: Who conducts elections to panchayats and municipalities?
questions.why: Under the 73rd and 74th Amendments, each state's State Election Commission conducts local body elections.

long.q: Distinguish between a direct election and an indirect election, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: direct election: voters themselves elect their representatives
B1: example: election of members of the Lok Sabha or a state Legislative Assembly
B1: indirect election: voters elect representatives, who in turn elect someone else
B1: example: election of the President, or of members of the Rajya Sabha

long.q: What is a mid-term election? Under what circumstance is one held?
scheme: B1: a mid-term election is an election to the whole Lok Sabha or a state Assembly held before its normal five-year term ends
B1: it is held when the House is dissolved early, for example when no party or coalition can form a stable government

long.q: Describe the composition of the Election Commission of India and the term of office of its members.
scheme: B1: it consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (at present two), appointed by the President
B1: they hold office for six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier
B1: the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only in the same way as a judge of the Supreme Court, which protects his independence

long.q: State any four functions of the Election Commission.
scheme: B1: preparing and revising the electoral rolls (voters' lists)
B1: recognising political parties and allotting election symbols
B1: fixing the election schedule and enforcing the Model Code of Conduct
B1: conducting elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President, and scrutinising nominations / appointing election officers

long.q: Name, in order, any five stages of an election in India after the dates are announced.
scheme: B1: issue of the notification calling the election
B1: filing of nomination papers by candidates
B1: scrutiny of nominations, then the last date for withdrawal
B1: election campaign, which stops 48 hours before polling
B1: polling, followed by counting of votes and declaration of results

questions.q: What is the minimum age to become a member of a state Legislative Assembly?
questions.why: A member of the Vidhan Sabha must be at least 25; for the Legislative Council the minimum is 30.

questions.q: The Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) of a state is:
o: a permanent House, with one-third of members retiring every two years
questions.why: Like the Rajya Sabha, the Council is never dissolved; members serve six years and one-third retire every second year.

questions.q: The Legislative Assembly of a state can have at most how many members?
questions.why: Article 170 fixes the strength at not more than 500 and not less than 60 (a few small states have fewer).

questions.q: Who appoints the Governor of a state?
o: The Chief Justice of the High Court
questions.why: The Governor is appointed by the President and holds office during the President's pleasure, normally for five years.

questions.q: How long can a Legislative Council hold up an ordinary bill already passed by the Assembly, at the most?
o: Four months in all (three months, then one month)
It can reject the bill permanently
questions.why: The Council can delay a bill for three months, and one more month if the Assembly passes it again; after that the bill is deemed passed.

long.q: Distinguish between a unicameral and a bicameral state legislature. Name two states that have a bicameral legislature.
scheme: B1: a unicameral legislature has only one House, the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha)
B1: a bicameral legislature has two Houses: the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)
B1: any two of: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana

long.q: How is a Legislative Council created or abolished in a state?
scheme: B1: the state Legislative Assembly passes a resolution to that effect
B1: the resolution must be passed by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting
B1: Parliament then passes a law to create or abolish the Council (Article 169)

long.q: Describe the composition of a state Legislative Council.
scheme: B1: one-third of the members are elected by members of the Legislative Assembly
B1: one-third are elected by local bodies such as municipalities and district boards
B1: one-twelfth are elected by graduates of three years' standing living in the state
B1: one-twelfth are elected by teachers of at least three years' standing in secondary schools and above
B1: one-sixth are nominated by the Governor from persons distinguished in literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service

long.q: State three financial powers of the state Legislative Assembly which show it is more powerful than the Legislative Council.
scheme: B1: a money bill can be introduced only in the Legislative Assembly
B1: the Council must return a money bill within 14 days, with or without recommendations, which the Assembly may reject
B1: the Assembly passes the state budget and controls the council of ministers, which is responsible to it alone

long.q: State any three legislative powers of the Governor in relation to the state legislature.
scheme: B1: the Governor summons and prorogues the Houses and can dissolve the Legislative Assembly
B1: no bill becomes law without the Governor's assent; the Governor may withhold assent, return a non-money bill, or reserve it for the President
B1: the Governor can issue ordinances when the legislature is not in session (Article 213) / addresses the legislature at the start of the first session each year

questions.q: Harappa, the first site of this civilisation to be excavated (1921), lies on the banks of which river?
questions.why: Harappa (now in Pakistani Punjab) is on the Ravi; Mohenjo-daro is on the Indus.

questions.q: Which Harappan site had a dockyard?
questions.why: Lothal in Gujarat had a brick dockyard linked to a river channel, showing sea trade.

questions.q: The Great Bath was found at which site?
questions.why: The Great Bath, a watertight brick tank probably used for ritual bathing, lies in the citadel of Mohenjo-daro.

questions.q: Most Harappan seals were made of:
questions.why: Seals were usually square tablets of steatite (soapstone), carved with an animal and a short script.

questions.q: Why is the Harappan civilisation called a Bronze Age civilisation?
o: Its people used tools made of copper and bronze but not iron
Its cities were built of bronze
It ended when bronze was discovered
questions.why: The people made tools, weapons and figures of copper and bronze; iron was unknown to them.

long.q: State any four features of town planning in Harappan cities.
scheme: B1: cities were divided into a raised citadel (west) and a larger lower town (east)
B1: streets were straight and crossed at right angles, dividing the town into rectangular blocks (grid pattern)
B1: houses were built of standard-sized burnt bricks, often with a courtyard, well and bathroom
B1: an efficient covered drainage system ran along the streets, with manholes for cleaning

long.q: Explain the importance of the Harappan seals as a source of history.
scheme: B1: seals carry figures of animals (such as the unicorn, bull, elephant), which show the animals the people knew and perhaps worshipped
B1: Harappan seals found in Mesopotamia show that the people traded with distant lands; seals were probably used to stamp goods
B1: they carry the Harappan script, which shows the people could write, though it has not been deciphered

long.q: What does the Great Granary tell us about the Harappan economy and administration?
scheme: B1: grain (wheat and barley) was produced in surplus and stored centrally, showing a strong agricultural base
B1: storing and distributing grain suggests an organised authority that collected grain, perhaps as tax, and paid workers

long.q: Give three pieces of evidence that the Harappans carried on trade with other regions.
scheme: B1: Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia, which refers to a land called Meluhha
B1: the dockyard at Lothal and finds of standard weights show organised trade
B1: raw materials such as gold, copper, tin and precious stones came from other regions, since they were not available locally

long.q: State any three possible causes of the decline of the Harappan civilisation.
scheme: B1: repeated floods, or change in the course of rivers such as the Indus
B1: drying up of rivers (such as the Ghaggar-Hakra) and a drier climate, causing desertification
B1: deforestation and overuse of land / earthquakes / outbreak of disease / decline of foreign trade

questions.q: Which is the oldest of the four Vedas?
questions.why: The Rig Veda, a collection of 1,028 hymns in ten mandalas, is the oldest Vedic text.

questions.q: Which Veda contains charms, spells and remedies for diseases?
questions.why: The Atharva Veda deals with everyday life: magic, charms and herbal medicine.

questions.q: In the Early Vedic period, the council of elders was called the:
questions.why: The Sabha was a council of elders; the Samiti was the larger popular assembly.

questions.q: The correct order of the four ashramas is:
questions.why: Life passed from student (Brahmacharya) to householder (Grihastha), to retreat (Vanaprastha) and finally renunciation (Sanyasa).

questions.q: Which of these women composed hymns of the Rig Veda?
questions.why: Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra and Vishwavara composed Rig Vedic hymns, showing women's high status in the Early Vedic age.

long.q: Name the four Vedas and state briefly what each one contains.
scheme: B1: Rig Veda: hymns in praise of gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna
B1: Sama Veda: hymns set to melody, to be sung at sacrifices (basis of Indian music)
B1: Yajur Veda: formulae and rules for performing sacrifices
B1: Atharva Veda: charms, spells and remedies for disease, reflecting popular beliefs

long.q: Describe the position of women in the Early Vedic period.
scheme: B1: women were respected, received education, and some composed hymns (Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra)
B1: they took part in religious ceremonies with their husbands and could attend the assemblies
B1: there was no child marriage and widows could remarry; women had some choice in marriage

long.q: How did the varna system change from the Early to the Later Vedic period?
scheme: B1: society was divided into four varnas: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras
B1: in the Early Vedic period the division was based on occupation and was flexible; people could change occupation
B1: in the Later Vedic period it became rigid and based on birth, and the Shudras were given the lowest position

long.q: Compare the economic life of the Early and Later Vedic periods.
scheme: B1: Early Vedic people were mainly pastoral; cattle were the main form of wealth
B1: in the Later Vedic period agriculture became the main occupation, helped by the iron ploughshare, and people settled in villages
B1: crafts and trade grew in the Later Vedic period (carpentry, metal work, weaving), and barter was the usual mode of exchange

long.q: State two features of education in the Vedic period.
scheme: B1: students lived in the gurukul (the teacher's home) and served the guru while studying
B1: education was oral; students learnt the Vedas, grammar, and also discipline and moral values

questions.q: Mahavira was the ______ Tirthankara of the Jains.
questions.why: Jains count 24 Tirthankaras; Rishabhanatha was the first, Parshvanatha the 23rd and Mahavira the 24th.

questions.q: Where did the Buddha deliver his first sermon?
questions.why: At the Deer Park in Sarnath, near Varanasi, he ‘set the wheel of law in motion’ (Dharmachakra Pravartana).

questions.q: The Tripitakas, the sacred texts of Buddhism, were written in which language?
questions.why: The three ‘baskets’ (Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma Pitaka) are in Pali; the Jain Angas are in Prakrit (Ardhamagadhi).

questions.q: The Jatakas are:
o: rules of discipline for Jain monks
stories of the previous births of the Buddha
questions.why: The Jatakas are tales of the Bodhisattva's earlier lives, which also tell us about society in that period.

questions.q: Which of these was a reason for the rise of new religions in the 6th century BC?
o: Vedic rituals had become costly and complicated
The Mauryan emperors banned Vedic religion
Foreign invaders forced people to convert
questions.why: Expensive sacrifices, Brahmanical dominance and the use of Sanskrit made people turn to simpler faiths taught in the people's languages.

long.q: Explain the Tri-ratnas (three jewels) of Jainism.
scheme: B1: Right Faith: belief in the teachings of the Tirthankaras
B1: Right Knowledge: true understanding of the teachings and of the nature of the soul
B1: Right Conduct: following the five vows in daily life; together the three lead to moksha (liberation)

long.q: State the Four Noble Truths taught by the Buddha.
scheme: B1: the world is full of suffering (dukkha)
B1: desire (craving) is the cause of suffering
B1: suffering can be ended by ending desire
B1: desire can be ended by following the Eightfold Path

long.q: Give any three reasons why Jainism and Buddhism became popular in the 6th century BC.
scheme: B1: Vedic religion had become full of costly rituals and animal sacrifices, which ordinary people could not afford
B1: the rigid caste system and the dominance of Brahmanas angered other groups such as Kshatriyas and Vaishyas
B1: the new faiths were simple and were preached in the people's languages (Pali and Prakrit), and they won royal patronage

long.q: Name the two sects into which Jainism split, and state one difference between them.
scheme: B1: Digambaras and Svetambaras
B1: Digambara monks give up clothes entirely (‘sky-clad’), while Svetambara monks wear white robes

long.q: Explain the Buddhist doctrine of the Middle Path and the idea of Nirvana.
scheme: B1: the Middle Path means avoiding both a life of luxury and extreme self-torture
B1: it is followed through the Eightfold Path: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration
B1: Nirvana is the final goal: freedom from desire and from the cycle of birth and death

questions.q: Who wrote the Arthashastra?
questions.why: Kautilya (Chanakya), adviser to Chandragupta Maurya, wrote this treatise on statecraft and administration.

questions.q: Megasthenes, author of the Indika, was the ambassador of:
questions.why: Seleucus Nicator sent Megasthenes to Chandragupta's court at Pataliputra after their treaty.

questions.q: Which Rock Edict of Ashoka describes the Kalinga War?
questions.why: Rock Edict XIII records the slaughter in Kalinga and Ashoka's remorse, which led him to Dhamma.

questions.q: Who first deciphered the Brahmi script of Ashoka's edicts?
questions.why: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837, making the edicts readable.

questions.q: Who succeeded Chandragupta Maurya?
questions.why: The order was Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara, then Ashoka.

long.q: Explain the importance of the Arthashastra and the Indika as sources of Mauryan history.
scheme: B1: the Arthashastra by Kautilya describes the duties of the king, ministers and officials
B1: it also gives details of taxation, the spy system, law and the economy
B1: the Indika by Megasthenes describes the city of Pataliputra and its administration by committees
B1: it also describes society and the king's court; although lost, it survives in quotations by later Greek writers

long.q: Describe the provincial and city administration of the Mauryas.
scheme: B1: the empire was divided into provinces, each under a prince (kumara) or viceroy
B1: provincial capitals included Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri; officials such as Rajukas and Pradeshikas worked under them
B1: according to Megasthenes, Pataliputra was run by 30 officials in six committees of five members each
B1: the committees looked after industry, foreigners, registration of births and deaths, trade, manufactured goods and collection of taxes

long.q: What were the main principles of Ashoka's Dhamma?
scheme: B1: respect for parents, elders and teachers, and kindness to servants and slaves
B1: non-violence: avoiding killing animals and ending wars of conquest
B1: tolerance and respect for all religions and sects
B1: truthfulness, charity and leading a moral life rather than performing empty rituals

long.q: State three steps Ashoka took to spread Dhamma.
scheme: B1: he had his teachings inscribed on rocks and pillars all over the empire, in the people's language
B1: he appointed officers called Dhamma Mahamatras to spread Dhamma and look after people's welfare
B1: he sent missionaries abroad, including his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka / he went on Dhamma tours himself

long.q: Why is the Sanchi Stupa an important source of Mauryan history?
scheme: B1: it was built under Ashoka (later enlarged), showing his support for Buddhism
B1: its carvings, especially on the gateways added later, show scenes from the Buddha's life and the Jatakas, and the life of the times

questions.q: The word ‘Sangam’ refers to:
o: an assembly of Tamil poets and scholars
questions.why: Sangams were assemblies of poets at Madurai, held under Pandya patronage.

questions.q: Who wrote the Tirukkural?
questions.why: Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural is a work of couplets on virtue, wealth and love.

questions.q: Which kingdom had Madurai as its capital and the fish as its emblem?
questions.why: The Pandyas ruled from Madurai with the fish emblem; the Cholas used the tiger and the Cheras the bow.

questions.q: Megaliths in South India are:
o: burial sites marked with large stones
questions.why: Megaliths are graves marked by big stones; the iron objects and pottery in them tell us about early Tamil life.

questions.q: Which of these was a major export from the Tamil country to Rome?
questions.why: Pepper, called ‘black gold’, was exported along with pearls, ivory and fine cloth; Roman coins have been found in the region.

long.q: Why is the Tirukkural an important source for the Sangam Age? State its three parts.
scheme: B1: it shows the moral and social values of the Tamils, and the duties of rulers, ministers and householders
B1: it is divided into three parts: Aram (virtue), Porul (wealth and polity) and Inbam (love)
B1: being written in couplets that are still read, it shows the high level of Tamil literature of the age

long.q: Describe the position of women in the Sangam Age.
scheme: B1: women were educated, and several women poets such as Avvaiyar composed Sangam poems
B1: they had freedom in choosing their partners and took part in economic activities such as farming and selling goods
B1: but widows lived a hard life, and among some of the upper classes the practice of sati existed

long.q: Explain how agriculture and trade flourished in the Sangam Age.
scheme: B1: fertile river valleys like the Kaveri delta produced rice, sugarcane, cotton and spices
B1: kings encouraged agriculture by building tanks and irrigation works
B1: there was flourishing trade with Rome and South-East Asia through ports such as Puhar, Muziris and Korkai
B1: finds of Roman coins and pottery at sites like Arikamedu prove this trade

long.q: Name the three kingdoms of the Sangam Age, with the capital of each.
scheme: B1: the Cholas, with their capital at Uraiyur (later Puhar)
B1: the Cheras, with their capital at Vanji
B1: the Pandyas, with their capital at Madurai

long.q: State two ways in which megaliths help historians understand the Sangam period.
scheme: B1: the iron tools, weapons and pottery buried in them show the people's crafts and the use of iron
B1: the different kinds of burial and the goods placed with the dead suggest belief in life after death and differences in social status

questions.q: Who composed the Allahabad Pillar Inscription praising Samudragupta?
questions.why: Harishena, Samudragupta's court poet, composed this prashasti describing his conquests.

questions.q: The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of:
questions.why: Fa-Hien travelled in India in the early 5th century, under Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya).

questions.q: Which Gupta ruler married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi?
questions.why: This marriage raised Chandragupta I's status; he took the title Maharajadhiraja and began the Gupta era (AD 319-320).

questions.q: Which mathematician of the Gupta age stated that the Earth rotates on its axis?
questions.why: In the Aryabhatiya, Aryabhata explained eclipses, rotation of the Earth and gave a close value of π.

questions.q: Why did historian V. A. Smith call Samudragupta the ‘Napoleon of India’?
o: Because of his many military conquests
Because he wrote a code of law
Because he was defeated in exile
questions.why: His long list of victories in the north and south, recorded on the Allahabad Pillar, reminded Smith of Napoleon.

long.q: Explain the importance of Fa-Hien's account as a source of Gupta history.
scheme: B1: he describes the people as prosperous and happy, and the government as mild, with light punishments
B1: he describes Buddhist monasteries and centres of learning, and the religious tolerance of the rulers
B1: he mentions that the Chandalas (untouchables) lived outside the towns, which shows social inequality

long.q: State three achievements of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya).
scheme: B1: he defeated the Shakas of western India, gaining Gujarat, Malwa and the western sea ports
B1: he made Ujjain a second capital and strengthened his position through marriage alliances (with the Vakatakas)
B1: his court was famous for learned men (the ‘Navaratnas’), including the poet Kalidasa

long.q: Describe the provincial and local administration of the Guptas.
scheme: B1: the empire was divided into provinces called bhuktis, each under an Uparika
B1: provinces were divided into districts called vishayas, under a Vishayapati
B1: the village was the smallest unit, run by a headman (gramika) with village elders

long.q: Name any two literary works of Kalidasa and explain why the Gupta period is called the ‘Golden Age’ of Indian culture.
scheme: B1: any two of: Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava
B1: Sanskrit literature flourished, with poets and playwrights such as Kalidasa
B1: great advances were made in science and mathematics (Aryabhata, Varahamihira), including the decimal place-value system and zero
B1: art and architecture flourished: Ajanta paintings, the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh, the Sarnath Buddha, and the Iron Pillar at Mehrauli

long.q: State two contributions of Varahamihira.
scheme: B1: he wrote the Pancha Siddhantika, summarising five systems of astronomy
B1: he wrote the Brihat Samhita, an encyclopaedia on astronomy, astrology, geography, plants and other subjects

questions.q: Who founded the imperial Chola line by capturing Thanjavur in the 9th century?
questions.why: Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur around AD 850 and made it the Chola capital.

questions.q: The Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur was built by:
questions.why: Rajaraja I completed the temple, a masterpiece of the Dravida style, around AD 1010.

questions.q: Why did Rajendra I take the title ‘Gangaikonda’?
o: He built a canal from the Ganga
He led a victorious expedition up to the Ganga
He was born on the banks of the Ganga
questions.why: After his northern campaign reached the Ganga, he founded a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram.

questions.q: The Uttaramerur inscriptions are important because they describe:
o: the working of village assemblies and elections
questions.why: They explain how members of village committees were chosen by lot (kudavolai) and who was qualified.

questions.q: The village assembly in villages granted to Brahmanas was called the:
questions.why: The Ur was the general village assembly, the Sabha or Mahasabha that of Brahmana villages, and the Nagaram that of merchants.

long.q: Describe the Chola system of local self-government in villages.
scheme: B1: there were assemblies such as the Ur (ordinary villages), the Sabha (Brahmana villages) and the Nagaram (merchants)
B1: the Sabha worked through committees (variyams) for gardens, tanks, justice and so on
B1: members were chosen by lot (kudavolai): names on palm leaves were put in a pot and drawn by a boy
B1: candidates had to own land, be of a set age and have knowledge of the Vedas; those who had not given accounts were disqualified

long.q: State three achievements of Rajendra I.
scheme: B1: he completed the conquest of Sri Lanka
B1: he led an expedition to the Ganga, took the title Gangaikonda and built Gangaikonda Cholapuram
B1: he sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya kingdom of South-East Asia (Kadaram)

long.q: Give three features of the Dravida style of temple architecture under the Cholas.
scheme: B1: a tall pyramid-shaped tower (vimana) rises over the main shrine (garbhagriha)
B1: temples have large pillared halls (mandapas) and huge gateways (gopurams) set in walled enclosures
B1: walls are richly carved with sculptures of gods and scenes from legends, as at the Brihadeshwara temple

long.q: Why are the Chola bronze images famous? Name the most famous one.
scheme: B1: they were made by the lost-wax process and are admired for their grace, balance and fine detail
B1: the image of Nataraja (Shiva as the cosmic dancer)

long.q: Explain how temples were centres of economic and social life under the Cholas.
scheme: B1: temples owned land and received grants, so they employed many people: priests, musicians, dancers, craftsmen
B1: they acted like banks, lending money and receiving deposits
B1: they were centres of learning, music, dance and festivals, and fed the poor

questions.q: Who began building the Qutb Minar?
questions.why: Aibak laid the foundation around 1199; Iltutmish completed it.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate?
questions.why: The Slave (Mamluk) dynasty was followed by the Khaljis, Tughlaqs, Sayyids and Lodis (1206 to 1526).

questions.q: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta came to India during the reign of:
questions.why: Ibn Battuta served as qazi of Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq and described his court in the Rehla.

questions.q: Which ruler introduced the system of branding horses (dagh) and keeping descriptive rolls of soldiers (huliya)?
questions.why: Alauddin Khalji did this to stop soldiers bringing poor horses or proxies at muster.

questions.q: Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted his capital from Delhi to:
questions.why: He moved the capital to Daulatabad (Devagiri) in the Deccan in 1327, but later had to move back.

long.q: Explain the importance of the Qutb Minar as a source of the Delhi Sultanate period.
scheme: B1: it was begun by Qutbuddin Aibak and completed by Iltutmish, so it tells us about these early Sultans
B1: its inscriptions in Arabic and Persian give historical information about the rulers who built or repaired it
B1: its style, with calligraphy and red and buff sandstone, shows the beginnings of Indo-Islamic architecture

long.q: Describe the market reforms of Alauddin Khalji.
scheme: B1: he fixed the prices of all goods, from grain and cloth to horses and slaves
B1: separate markets were set up for grain, cloth, horses and cattle, each under an officer (Shahna-i-Mandi)
B1: grain was stored in government granaries to prevent shortages and hoarding
B1: spies reported on traders, and those who cheated or used false weights were severely punished

long.q: Why did Muhammad bin Tughlaq transfer his capital to Daulatabad? Why did the plan fail?
scheme: B1: Daulatabad was centrally placed, so the south as well as the north could be controlled
B1: it was safer from Mongol attacks on Delhi
B1: the plan failed because the whole population of Delhi was forced to move about 1,100 km in hot weather, and many died on the way
B1: from Daulatabad the north-west frontier could not be guarded, so the capital had to be moved back to Delhi

long.q: What was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency? Why did it fail?
scheme: B1: he issued copper (or brass) coins with the same value as silver coins
B1: the government could not stop people from forging the coins in their homes
B1: markets were flooded with false coins, trade collapsed, and the Sultan had to exchange them for gold and silver coins, emptying the treasury

long.q: Name two literary sources for the history of the Delhi Sultanate and their authors.
scheme: B1: Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi by Ziauddin Barani / Tabaqat-i-Nasiri by Minhaj-us-Siraj
B1: the Rehla by Ibn Battuta / works of Amir Khusrau

questions.q: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in which battle?
questions.why: At Panipat in April 1526, Babur's artillery and tulughma tactics defeated Ibrahim Lodi and founded Mughal rule.

questions.q: Who wrote the Akbarnama and the Ain-i-Akbari?
questions.why: Abul Fazl, Akbar's friend and courtier, wrote the official history of the reign and its account of administration.

questions.q: In the mansabdari system, the ‘sawar’ rank showed:
o: the number of horsemen he had to maintain
questions.why: Zat fixed personal rank and pay; sawar fixed the cavalry he had to keep.

questions.q: Which of these was part of Akbar's policy towards the Rajputs?
o: He abolished the pilgrim tax and the jizya
He made Persian compulsory in Rajput states
He imposed a new tax on Hindus
questions.why: He abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564), married into Rajput families and gave Rajputs high posts.

questions.q: The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was built to celebrate Akbar's conquest of:
questions.why: Akbar built the great gateway after his victory in Gujarat (1573).

long.q: Name the three battles fought by Babur in India and the opponent in each.
scheme: B1: First Battle of Panipat (1526) against Ibrahim Lodi
B1: Battle of Khanwa (1527) against Rana Sanga of Mewar
B1: Battle of Ghaghra (1529) against the Afghans of Bihar and Bengal under Mahmud Lodi

long.q: Explain any four features of the mansabdari system of Akbar.
scheme: B1: every officer was given a mansab (rank), which fixed his status, salary and military duties
B1: each mansabdar held a zat rank (personal) and a sawar rank (number of horsemen)
B1: ranks ranged from 10 to 10,000 (higher ones were for princes); mansabdars were appointed, promoted or dismissed by the emperor
B1: they were paid in cash or by assignment of jagirs; the post was not hereditary

long.q: Describe Akbar's religious policy.
scheme: B1: he followed sulh-i-kul (peace with all) and gave equal treatment to all religions
B1: he built the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri (1575) for discussions among scholars of different faiths
B1: by the Mahzar (1579) he became the final authority in religious disputes
B1: he introduced Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi), a path drawing on the best in all religions, which only a few courtiers joined

long.q: Why did Akbar adopt a policy of friendship towards the Rajputs? State two results of this policy.
scheme: B1: the Rajputs were brave warriors; making them friends would strengthen the empire and secure the frontier
B1: he wanted a broad base of support among Indians, not only among Turkish and Afghan nobles
B1: result: Rajputs such as Raja Man Singh and Raja Todar Mal served the empire loyally in high posts
B1: result: most Rajput states accepted Mughal rule; only Mewar, under Rana Pratap, held out

long.q: Name two monuments of the Mughal period and the emperor who built each.
scheme: B1: Fatehpur Sikri with the Buland Darwaza, built by Akbar
B1: the Taj Mahal at Agra / the Red Fort and Jama Masjid at Delhi, built by Shah Jahan

questions.q: The Bijak is a collection of the teachings of:
questions.why: Kabir's dohas and songs are collected in the Bijak; some also appear in the Guru Granth Sahib.

questions.q: The Adi Granth was compiled by:
questions.why: Guru Arjan Dev compiled it in 1604; with additions it became the Guru Granth Sahib.

questions.q: The dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti is at:
questions.why: Moinuddin Chishti, founder of the Chishti order in India, settled at Ajmer.

questions.q: A Sufi hospice where the saint lived with disciples was called a:
questions.why: Sufis lived in khanqahs, where they taught, held sama (music) and fed visitors.

questions.q: Which Christian missionary arrived in Goa in 1542?
questions.why: Francis Xavier, a founder member of the Jesuits, worked in Goa and along the coast.

long.q: What is meant by composite culture? State two factors that helped it grow in medieval India.
scheme: B1: composite culture is a culture formed by the blending of elements from different religions and communities, here Hindu and Islamic traditions
B1: the Bhakti and Sufi saints preached love, devotion and equality, bringing people of different faiths together
B1: rulers such as Akbar encouraged tolerance; intermarriage, trade and the use of common languages also helped

long.q: State three teachings of Kabir.
scheme: B1: God is one; Rama and Rahim are different names of the same God
B1: he rejected idol worship, rituals, pilgrimages and fasting as the path to God
B1: he condemned the caste system and preached that devotion and a pure heart lead to God

long.q: Give three teachings of Guru Nanak.
scheme: B1: there is one God, formless and everywhere, who should be remembered through his name (naam)
B1: all human beings are equal, whatever their caste, religion or sex; he started the langar (community kitchen)
B1: one should lead an honest householder's life, earn by honest work and share with others

long.q: Explain any four features of the Sufi movement.
scheme: B1: Sufis believed in love and devotion to God as the way to reach him
B1: they were organised into orders (silsilas) such as the Chishti and Suhrawardi
B1: a disciple (murid) followed a spiritual guide (pir), and Sufis lived in khanqahs
B1: they used music and song (sama, qawwali) in worship and served all people, whatever their religion

long.q: State two ways in which composite culture is seen in language and architecture.
scheme: B1: Urdu developed from a mix of Persian, Arabic and Hindi words
B1: Indo-Islamic architecture combined arches, domes and minarets with Indian features such as brackets, chhatris and lotus motifs (e.g. Fatehpur Sikri)

topics.name: The Modern Age in Europe: Renaissance

questions.q: The word ‘Renaissance’ means:
questions.why: It is French for ‘rebirth’, the revival of classical Greek and Roman learning and art.

questions.q: The Renaissance began in which country?
questions.why: It began in the Italian cities, especially Florence, in the 14th century.

questions.q: The capture of Constantinople by the Ottoman Turks in 1453 helped the Renaissance because:
o: Greek scholars fled to Italy with their manuscripts
it opened a new land route to India
the Turks paid for new universities
questions.why: The scholars who fled spread Greek learning in Italy.

questions.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.why: Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512; he also carved the statue of David.

questions.q: Who put forward the theory that the Earth and the planets move round the Sun?
questions.why: Copernicus set out the heliocentric theory in 1543; Galileo later supported it with telescope observations.

long.q: Explain how the invention of the printing press helped the Renaissance.
scheme: B1: Gutenberg's press (about 1450) made books cheap and plentiful
B1: new ideas and classical works reached many more people, not just the clergy and the rich
B1: it encouraged the use of vernacular languages and spread the spirit of inquiry and criticism

long.q: State any four causes of the Renaissance.
scheme: B1: the fall of Constantinople (1453), which sent Greek scholars and manuscripts to Italy
B1: the invention of printing, which spread learning
B1: the growth of trade and of rich towns, whose merchants and rulers (such as the Medici) became patrons of art and learning
B1: the Crusades, which brought Europeans into contact with the East / decline of feudalism / geographical discoveries

long.q: What is humanism? Name the scholar called the ‘father of humanism’.
scheme: B1: humanism was a way of thinking that valued human beings, their life in this world and their abilities, and drew on classical learning, rather than concentrating only on religion and the afterlife
B1: Petrarch

long.q: Name two great writers of the Renaissance and one work by each.
scheme: B1: Dante: The Divine Comedy / Machiavelli: The Prince / Erasmus: In Praise of Folly
B1: Thomas More: Utopia / Cervantes: Don Quixote / Shakespeare: any of his plays

long.q: Describe three changes the Renaissance brought to art.
scheme: B1: art became realistic: artists studied anatomy and painted the human body accurately
B1: they used perspective and light and shade, giving depth to paintings, e.g. Leonardo's Last Supper
B1: subjects included ordinary people and nature as well as religion, and artists were supported by rich patrons rather than only the Church

topics.name: The Modern Age in Europe: Reformation

questions.q: Martin Luther nailed his 95 Theses to the church door at Wittenberg in:
questions.why: On 31 October 1517 he attacked the sale of indulgences, starting the Reformation.

questions.q: An indulgence was:
o: a certificate sold by the Church that was said to reduce punishment for sins
questions.why: Agents such as Johann Tetzel sold indulgences to raise money for the Church.

questions.q: Who founded the Society of Jesus (the Jesuits)?
questions.why: The Jesuits, founded by Loyola and approved in 1540, led the Counter-Reformation through education and missions.

questions.q: John Wycliffe, called the ‘Morning Star of the Reformation’, worked in:
questions.why: Wycliffe criticised the Church in 14th-century England and had the Bible translated into English.

questions.q: The Council of Trent (1545-1563) was part of:
questions.why: The Catholic Church called it to reform itself and to restate its doctrines against Protestantism.

long.q: What is meant by the Reformation? State three of its causes.
scheme: B1: the Reformation was the 16th-century movement to reform the Catholic Church; it led to the rise of Protestant churches
B1: corruption in the Church, such as the sale of indulgences and church posts, and the worldly lives of many clergy
B1: kings and princes resented the Pope's interference and the Church's wealth and taxes
B1: the Renaissance spirit of questioning and the printing press, which spread critical ideas

long.q: Describe Martin Luther's role in the Reformation.
scheme: B1: in 1517 he posted his 95 Theses at Wittenberg, attacking the sale of indulgences
B1: he taught that a person is saved by faith alone, and that the Bible, not the Pope, is the final authority
B1: he refused to withdraw his views, was excommunicated (1521) and declared an outlaw at the Diet of Worms
B1: he translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it, and his followers came to be called Protestants

long.q: State three measures taken by the Catholic Church in the Counter-Reformation.
scheme: B1: the Council of Trent restated Catholic doctrines and ended abuses such as the sale of church posts
B1: the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) spread Catholic faith through schools and missions
B1: the Inquisition punished heretics, and an Index of books Catholics were forbidden to read was issued

long.q: Name two other reformers besides Martin Luther and the country in which each worked.
scheme: B1: John Calvin in Geneva (Switzerland) / Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich (Switzerland)
B1: John Wycliffe in England / John Huss in Bohemia

long.q: State three results of the Reformation.
scheme: B1: the unity of the Christian Church in Western Europe was broken; Protestant churches were set up
B1: kings became more powerful as the Pope's authority declined, which helped the rise of nation states (e.g. Church of England under Henry VIII)
B1: the Catholic Church reformed itself, and education and the use of vernacular languages spread

topics.name: The Modern Age in Europe: Industrial Revolution

questions.q: The Industrial Revolution began in which country?
questions.why: It began in England in the second half of the 18th century.

questions.q: Who invented the spinning jenny?
questions.why: Hargreaves invented it around 1764; it let one worker spin many threads at once.

questions.q: James Watt is famous for:
questions.why: Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1769) was efficient enough to drive factory machines.

questions.q: Who wrote the Communist Manifesto (1848) with Friedrich Engels?
questions.why: Marx and Engels called on workers to end capitalism; their ideas shaped socialism.

questions.q: Which of these helped England industrialise first?
o: Large deposits of coal and iron close together
questions.why: Coal and iron near each other, capital from trade, colonies and a large navy gave England a head start.

long.q: What is meant by the Industrial Revolution? State three reasons why it began in England.
scheme: B1: the Industrial Revolution was the change from production by hand at home to production by machines in factories, starting in the 18th century
B1: England had rich deposits of coal and iron, often close together
B1: England had capital from trade and colonies that supplied raw materials and markets
B1: the agricultural revolution and enclosures released labour for factories / political stability and a strong navy

long.q: Name the inventor of each of the following: (a) flying shuttle (b) water frame (c) spinning mule (d) power loom.
scheme: B1: flying shuttle: John Kay (1733)
B1: water frame: Richard Arkwright (1769)
B1: spinning mule: Samuel Crompton (1779)
B1: power loom: Edmund Cartwright (1785)

long.q: Explain the meaning of capitalism and state two of its features.
scheme: B1: capitalism is an economic system in which the means of production (factories, machines, land) are privately owned and run for profit
B1: the owners (capitalists) hire workers for wages and keep the profits
B1: prices and production are set by free competition in the market, with little government control

long.q: Why did socialism arise during the Industrial Revolution? State two of its aims.
scheme: B1: factory workers worked long hours for low wages in unsafe conditions, while owners grew rich
B1: thinkers such as Robert Owen and Karl Marx argued that this system was unjust
B1: aim: the means of production should be owned by society or the state, not by private individuals
B1: aim: wealth should be distributed fairly so as to end exploitation and class differences

long.q: State three effects of the Industrial Revolution on society.
scheme: B1: people moved from villages to industrial towns, which grew fast and became crowded, with slums
B1: a new working class and a rich middle class of factory owners arose
B1: workers, including women and children, faced long hours and poor conditions, which led to trade unions and labour laws

questions.q: The Parliament of India consists of:
o: the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha only
the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha
the Prime Minister and the two Houses
the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the Supreme Court
questions.why: Article 79: Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses.

questions.q: How many members can the President nominate to the Rajya Sabha?
questions.why: Twelve members with special knowledge of literature, science, art or social service are nominated.

questions.q: Who presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
questions.why: Under Article 108 the Speaker presides over a joint sitting held to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary bill.

questions.q: Within how many days must the Rajya Sabha return a money bill?
questions.why: If the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days, the bill is deemed passed by both Houses.

questions.q: What is the minimum age to become a member of the Rajya Sabha?
questions.why: It is 30 for the Rajya Sabha and 25 for the Lok Sabha.

long.q: State the term of the Lok Sabha. Under what circumstance can it be extended, and for how long?
scheme: B1: the normal term of the Lok Sabha is five years from its first meeting
B1: it can be extended during a proclamation of national emergency
B1: by a law of Parliament, for one year at a time, and not beyond six months after the emergency ends

long.q: Explain the following: (a) Question Hour (b) Zero Hour (c) adjournment motion.
scheme: B1: Question Hour: usually the first hour of a sitting, when members ask ministers questions about their ministries
B1: Zero Hour: the time just after Question Hour when members raise urgent matters without prior notice
B1: adjournment motion: a motion to set aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance

long.q: How is a money bill passed in Parliament? Who decides whether a bill is a money bill?
scheme: B1: a money bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only on the recommendation of the President
B1: after the Lok Sabha passes it, it goes to the Rajya Sabha, which must return it within 14 days
B1: the Lok Sabha may accept or reject the Rajya Sabha's recommendations; the bill then goes to the President, who cannot refuse assent
B1: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha decides whether a bill is a money bill, and the decision is final

long.q: State any three ways in which Parliament controls the executive.
scheme: B1: through questions and supplementary questions to ministers
B1: through motions such as adjournment motions and cut motions on the budget
B1: the Lok Sabha can remove the Council of Ministers by passing a no-confidence motion

long.q: Mention two special powers of the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha does not have.
scheme: B1: by a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting, it can allow Parliament to make laws on a subject in the State List (Article 249)
B1: by a similar resolution, it can authorise Parliament to create new All-India Services (Article 312)

topics.name: The Union Executive: The President and the Vice-President

questions.q: The President of India is elected by:
o: the members of the Lok Sabha only
the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the state Legislative Assemblies
questions.why: The electoral college includes elected MPs and elected MLAs (including those of Delhi and Puducherry).

questions.q: The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of:
questions.why: The Vice-President presides over the Rajya Sabha.

questions.q: Under which Article can the President proclaim a national emergency?
questions.why: 352 is national emergency, 356 failure of constitutional machinery in a state, 360 financial emergency.

questions.q: When Parliament is not in session, the President can make law through:
questions.why: Under Article 123 the President can issue ordinances, which must be approved within six weeks of Parliament reassembling.

questions.q: An impeachment resolution against the President must be passed by:
o: a simple majority of members present in the Lok Sabha
a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House
questions.why: Article 61 requires two-thirds of the total membership of the House that passes the charge, and then of the House that investigates it.

long.q: State the qualifications needed to be elected President of India.
scheme: B1: the person must be a citizen of India and at least 35 years old
B1: must be qualified to be elected a member of the Lok Sabha
B1: must not hold any office of profit under the Central or a state government

long.q: Why is the President elected indirectly and not directly by the people? Give two reasons.
scheme: B1: the President is only a constitutional head; a direct election would give him a separate mandate and could create a rival centre of power to the Prime Minister
B1: a direct election in such a large country would be very costly and time-consuming

long.q: Describe the procedure for the impeachment of the President.
scheme: B1: the President can be impeached only for violation of the Constitution
B1: the charge must be signed by at least one-fourth of the members of either House, and 14 days' notice given
B1: the resolution must be passed by two-thirds of the total membership of that House
B1: the other House then investigates; if it too passes the resolution by a two-thirds majority, the President is removed

long.q: State any four executive or legislative powers of the President.
scheme: B1: appoints the Prime Minister and, on his advice, the other ministers
B1: appoints Governors, judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Attorney General and the Chief Election Commissioner
B1: summons and prorogues the Houses of Parliament and can dissolve the Lok Sabha
B1: gives assent to bills (or returns non-money bills) and can issue ordinances / nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha

long.q: State the qualifications, term and the manner of election of the Vice-President.
scheme: B1: must be a citizen, at least 35 years old, and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha
B1: term is five years, and the Vice-President can be re-elected
B1: elected by an electoral college of all members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament, by proportional representation with a single transferable vote

topics.name: The Union Executive: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers

questions.q: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to:
questions.why: Article 75(3): if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the whole ministry must resign.

questions.q: The total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, cannot exceed what percentage of the strength of the Lok Sabha?
questions.why: The 91st Amendment (2003) set this limit.

questions.q: A person who is not a member of Parliament can be appointed a minister, but must become one within:
questions.why: Otherwise he or she must stop being a minister after six months.

questions.q: Which is the correct statement about the Cabinet?
o: It is larger than the Council of Ministers
It is a small body of senior ministers within the Council of Ministers
It is elected by the Rajya Sabha
questions.why: The Cabinet is the inner group of Cabinet ministers; it takes the main policy decisions.

questions.q: Who appoints the Prime Minister?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Lok Sabha by secret ballot
questions.why: The President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha.

long.q: Explain the meaning of collective responsibility and individual responsibility of ministers.
scheme: B1: collective responsibility: the Council of Ministers works as a team and is responsible as a whole to the Lok Sabha
B1: a decision of the Cabinet is binding on all ministers; if the Lok Sabha passes a vote of no confidence, the whole ministry resigns
B1: individual responsibility: each minister is responsible for the work of his or her own ministry
B1: ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, who can remove a minister on the Prime Minister's advice

long.q: Distinguish between the Cabinet and the Council of Ministers on three points.
scheme: B1: the Council of Ministers is a large body of all ministers (Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers); the Cabinet is a small body of senior ministers
B1: the Cabinet meets regularly and takes policy decisions; the Council of Ministers rarely meets as a body
B1: the Cabinet's decisions are binding on the whole Council of Ministers

long.q: State any four powers and functions of the Prime Minister.
scheme: B1: forms the Council of Ministers by recommending names to the President, and allocates portfolios
B1: presides over Cabinet meetings and coordinates the work of the ministries
B1: acts as the link between the President and the Cabinet, informing the President of decisions (Article 78)
B1: is the leader of the Lok Sabha / can advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha / advises on major appointments

long.q: State any three functions of the Cabinet.
scheme: B1: it decides the policies of the government, both domestic and foreign
B1: it prepares bills and the budget and guides them through Parliament
B1: it coordinates the work of different ministries and advises the President on appointments and the use of emergency powers

long.q: Why is the President bound to act on the advice of the Council of Ministers?
scheme: B1: Article 74 (as amended by the 42nd and 44th Amendments) says the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers, though he may once return advice for reconsideration
B1: India has a parliamentary system: the real executive power lies with the ministers, who are responsible to the elected Lok Sabha, while the President is a nominal head

questions.q: At what age does a judge of the Supreme Court retire?
questions.why: Supreme Court judges retire at 65; High Court judges at 62.

questions.q: The Supreme Court's power to give its opinion on a question referred by the President is its:
questions.why: Under Article 143 the President may seek its advice; the advice is not binding.

questions.q: A dispute between the Government of India and one or more states comes under the Supreme Court's:
questions.why: Under Article 131 such federal disputes can be heard only by the Supreme Court, starting there.

questions.q: The collegium that recommends judges for the Supreme Court consists of:
o: the Prime Minister and the Law Minister
the President and the Chief Justice
the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most judges
all the judges of the Supreme Court
questions.why: The collegium came from the Judges cases (1993, 1998); the NJAC that was to replace it was struck down in 2015.

questions.q: Calling the Supreme Court a ‘court of record’ means that:
o: its judgments are recorded and used as precedents, and it can punish for contempt of itself
it can only hear recorded evidence
questions.why: Article 129 makes its records evidence of law and gives it power to punish for contempt.

long.q: State the qualifications for appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court.
scheme: B1: must be a citizen of India
B1: must have been a judge of a High Court for at least five years, or an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years
B1: or must be, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist

long.q: How can a judge of the Supreme Court be removed?
scheme: B1: only on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity
B1: a motion must be passed in each House of Parliament by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting
B1: the President then issues the order of removal in the same session

long.q: State four provisions that ensure the independence of the judiciary.
scheme: B1: security of tenure: judges can be removed only by a difficult process of Parliament
B1: salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and cannot be reduced to their disadvantage during their term (except in a financial emergency)
B1: the conduct of judges cannot be discussed in Parliament except during a removal motion
B1: retired Supreme Court judges cannot practise law in any court in India / appointments are made on the recommendation of the collegium

long.q: Explain the writ jurisdiction and the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
scheme: B1: writ jurisdiction: under Article 32 the Court can issue writs such as habeas corpus and mandamus to enforce Fundamental Rights
B1: so a citizen whose Fundamental Rights are violated can go straight to the Supreme Court
B1: appellate jurisdiction: it hears appeals against judgments of High Courts in constitutional, civil and criminal cases
B1: in criminal cases, for example, an appeal lies where a High Court has reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death, or certifies that the case is fit for appeal

long.q: What is meant by judicial review? Why is it important?
scheme: B1: judicial review is the power of the courts to examine laws and executive orders and declare them void if they go against the Constitution
B1: it protects the Fundamental Rights of citizens from being taken away by the legislature or executive
B1: it keeps the Union and the states within their powers and makes the Supreme Court the guardian of the Constitution

topics.name: The Judiciary: High Courts and Subordinate Courts

questions.q: At what age does a High Court judge retire?
questions.why: High Court judges retire at 62.

questions.q: When the District Judge hears criminal cases, the court is called the:
questions.why: The same judge is the District Judge in civil cases and the Sessions Judge in criminal cases.

questions.q: Which statement about Lok Adalats is correct?
o: Their decisions can be appealed in the Supreme Court
They settle disputes by compromise and charge no court fee
questions.why: Lok Adalats, given statutory status by the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, settle cases quickly by mutual agreement; their award is final.

questions.q: Under which Article can a High Court issue writs?
questions.why: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and ‘for any other purpose’, a wider power than under Article 32.

questions.q: A death sentence passed by a Sessions Court:
o: is final and cannot be questioned
must be confirmed by the President first
must be confirmed by the High Court before it is carried out
is reviewed by the Lok Adalat
questions.why: The High Court must confirm any death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court.

long.q: State the qualifications for appointment as a judge of a High Court.
scheme: B1: must be a citizen of India
B1: must have held a judicial office in India for at least ten years, or been an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years

long.q: Describe the original and supervisory jurisdiction of a High Court.
scheme: B1: original jurisdiction: it can issue writs under Article 226 to enforce Fundamental Rights and for other legal rights
B1: it also hears certain cases directly, such as election petitions and some matters relating to marriage, wills and company law
B1: supervisory jurisdiction: under Article 227 it supervises all subordinate courts and tribunals in its area
B1: it can call for records, transfer cases, and make rules for the working of these courts

long.q: Explain why the High Court is called a court of record.
scheme: B1: its judgments are recorded and are binding on the subordinate courts in its territory, and can be cited as precedents
B1: it has the power to punish for contempt of itself (Article 215)

long.q: Name the civil courts and the criminal courts in a district, from highest to lowest.
scheme: B1: civil: Court of the District Judge
B1: civil: Court of the Civil Judge (Senior Division / Sub-Judge) and Civil Judge (Junior Division / Munsif); small cause courts for petty cases
B1: criminal: Sessions Court (Sessions Judge and Additional Sessions Judges)
B1: criminal: Courts of the Chief Judicial Magistrate and Judicial Magistrates of the first and second class

long.q: State three advantages of Lok Adalats.
scheme: B1: cases are settled quickly, reducing the backlog in regular courts
B1: no court fee is charged, and the procedure is simple and informal, so the poor benefit
B1: disputes are settled by compromise, so the parties remain on good terms, and the award is final with no appeal

questions.q: The revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on:
questions.why: Sepoys at Meerut rose on 10 May 1857 and marched to Delhi; Mangal Pandey's protest at Barrackpore was earlier, on 29 March.

questions.q: Under the Doctrine of Lapse, which state was annexed in 1853?
questions.why: Dalhousie annexed Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854) under this doctrine; Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the charge of misgovernment.

questions.q: Who led the revolt at Lucknow?
questions.why: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the rising in Awadh and proclaimed her son ruler.

questions.q: The immediate cause of the revolt was:
o: the greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle
questions.why: Sepoys believed the cartridges, which had to be bitten open, were greased with cow and pig fat, offending both Hindus and Muslims.

questions.q: Which Act of 1858 ended the rule of the East India Company?
questions.why: It transferred power to the British Crown, to be exercised through a Secretary of State for India.

long.q: State three political causes of the revolt of 1857.
scheme: B1: the Doctrine of Lapse, under which states such as Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur were annexed when a ruler died without a natural heir
B1: the annexation of Awadh in 1856 on the charge of misgovernment, which angered sepoys, many of whom came from Awadh
B1: the stopping of Nana Saheb's pension and the announcement that the Mughal emperor's successors would lose the title and the Red Fort

long.q: Explain any three military causes of the revolt.
scheme: B1: Indian sepoys got lower pay than British soldiers and could not rise to high ranks
B1: the General Service Enlistment Act (1856) required sepoys to serve overseas, which went against the religious beliefs of many
B1: the withdrawal of the foreign service allowance (batta) and the use of the new greased cartridges

long.q: State any three social and religious causes of the revolt.
scheme: B1: reforms such as the abolition of sati and the Widow Remarriage Act (1856) were seen as interference with religion
B1: Christian missionaries were active and allowed to convert people, sometimes with official support
B1: the Religious Disabilities Act (1850) allowed a convert to inherit ancestral property, which people saw as encouraging conversion

long.q: State four consequences of the revolt of 1857.
scheme: B1: the East India Company's rule ended, and India came under the British Crown (Government of India Act, 1858)
B1: a Secretary of State for India, with a Council of India, was appointed, and the Governor-General was given the title of Viceroy
B1: the Doctrine of Lapse was given up and the princes were assured their states would not be annexed
B1: the army was reorganised: more British soldiers were kept, and regiments were mixed by caste and region to divide them

long.q: State two promises made in the Queen's Proclamation of 1 November 1858.
scheme: B1: the British would not annex any more Indian states and would respect the rights and dignity of the princes
B1: there would be no interference in the religious beliefs of Indians, and Indians would be admitted to government posts on merit, regardless of race or creed

topics.name: Growth of Nationalism and the Founding of the Indian National Congress

questions.q: Who put forward the ‘Drain Theory’ in his book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India?
questions.why: Naoroji argued that Britain drained India's wealth through salaries, pensions and profits sent home.

questions.q: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was passed by:
questions.why: Lytton's Act curbed newspapers in Indian languages, but not English papers.

questions.q: The Ilbert Bill (1883) aimed to:
o: allow Indian judges to try Europeans
questions.why: Under Lord Ripon, it proposed that Indian judges could try European offenders; Europeans' protests forced it to be diluted.

questions.q: Where was the first session of the Indian National Congress held in 1885?
questions.why: It met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, from 28 December 1885, with 72 delegates.

questions.q: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress?
questions.why: W. C. Bonnerjee was the first president; A. O. Hume, a retired civil servant, had helped found it.

long.q: How did Western education help the growth of nationalism in India?
scheme: B1: English became a common language through which educated Indians from different regions could communicate
B1: Indians read about the ideas of liberty, equality, democracy and nationalism from Western thinkers
B1: the educated class saw the contrast between these ideals and British rule in India and became leaders of the national movement

long.q: Explain how the repressive policies of Lord Lytton helped the growth of nationalism.
scheme: B1: the Vernacular Press Act (1878) muzzled the Indian-language press
B1: the Arms Act (1878) required Indians, but not Europeans, to have a licence to carry arms
B1: the grand Delhi Durbar (1877) was held while millions died in famine
B1: the maximum age for the ICS examination was lowered (to 19), making it harder for Indians to compete; all this showed racial discrimination and united Indians

long.q: Name any three political associations formed before the Indian National Congress, with their founders or place.
scheme: B1: the East India Association (1866), founded in London by Dadabhai Naoroji
B1: the Indian Association (1876), founded in Calcutta by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose
B1: the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) / Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) / Bombay Presidency Association (1885)

long.q: What was the ‘safety valve’ theory about the founding of the Congress?
scheme: B1: it is the view that A. O. Hume founded the Congress, with official approval, to give a harmless outlet to growing Indian discontent
B1: it was meant to prevent another violent outbreak like 1857 against British rule

long.q: State three ways in which the press and literature helped the growth of nationalism.
scheme: B1: newspapers such as the Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu and the Kesari criticised British policies and spread political awareness
B1: they carried news from one region to another, helping Indians think of themselves as one nation
B1: literature such as Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's Anandamath (with ‘Vande Mataram’) inspired patriotism

topics.name: The First Phase of the Indian National Movement (1885-1907)

questions.q: The early nationalists were also known as:
questions.why: They used moderate, constitutional methods and trusted British justice.

questions.q: The political methods of the early nationalists are often summed up as:
questions.why: They sent petitions, held meetings and passed resolutions to win reforms from the British.

questions.q: Who founded the Servants of India Society in 1905?
questions.why: Gokhale founded it to train dedicated workers for national service; Gandhiji regarded him as his political guru.

questions.q: Which Act of 1892 is considered an achievement of the early nationalists?
questions.why: It enlarged the legislative councils and allowed some members to be indirectly elected and to discuss the budget.

questions.q: Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian to be elected to:
questions.why: He was elected from Finsbury Central in 1892.

long.q: State any four demands of the early nationalists.
scheme: B1: expansion of the legislative councils with more elected Indian members
B1: holding the ICS examination in India as well as in England, and raising the age limit
B1: reduction of military expenditure and of land revenue
B1: separation of the judiciary from the executive / freedom of speech and press / protection of Indian industries

long.q: Explain any three methods used by the early nationalists.
scheme: B1: they believed in constitutional means: they sent petitions and memorandums to the government
B1: they held meetings and passed resolutions at Congress sessions to educate public opinion
B1: they tried to influence British public opinion by sending delegations to England and through newspapers there

long.q: State three achievements of the early nationalists.
scheme: B1: they created political awareness and a sense of national unity among Indians
B1: their economic critique (the Drain Theory) exposed how British rule impoverished India
