B1: they won some reforms, such as the Indian Councils Act of 1892, and trained Indians in political work

long.q: Give three reasons why the early nationalists believed in British justice and loyalty to the Crown.
scheme: B1: they were educated in Western ideas and admired British liberal institutions and democracy
B1: they believed British rule had brought benefits like modern education, railways and the rule of law
B1: they thought the British would grant reforms once they knew the true conditions of India

long.q: State two contributions of Surendranath Banerjee to the national movement.
scheme: B1: he founded the Indian Association (1876) and toured India to protest against the lowering of the ICS age limit
B1: he used the press (his paper The Bengalee) and was twice Congress president; he led the protest against the Partition of Bengal

topics.name: The Second Phase of the Indian National Movement (1905-1916)

questions.q: The Partition of Bengal came into effect on:
questions.why: Curzon's partition took effect on 16 October 1905, observed as a day of mourning.

questions.q: The slogan ‘Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it’ is associated with:
questions.why: Tilak, editor of the Kesari and the Mahratta, was a leading assertive nationalist.

questions.q: The split in the Congress between the Moderates and the Assertive Nationalists took place at:
questions.why: The Surat session of 1907 broke up over the choice of president and the programme; the two groups reunited at Lucknow in 1916.

questions.q: Which of these was a feature of the Lucknow Pact of 1916?
o: The Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims
questions.why: The Congress and the League agreed on joint demands, and the Congress accepted separate electorates.

questions.q: Annie Besant started her Home Rule League in 1916 at:
questions.why: Tilak's league (April 1916) worked in Maharashtra and Karnataka; Besant's (September 1916) in the rest of India, from Madras.

long.q: State the reasons given by Lord Curzon for the Partition of Bengal, and its real motive.
scheme: B1: official reason: the province of Bengal was too large to be administered by one government
B1: real motive: Bengal was the centre of the national movement, and partition would weaken it
B1: by creating a Muslim-majority East Bengal, the British wanted to divide Hindus and Muslims (divide and rule)

long.q: Explain the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement.
scheme: B1: it began as a protest against the Partition of Bengal (1905)
B1: boycott meant refusing British goods, especially cloth, which were burnt in public bonfires
B1: swadeshi meant using Indian-made goods, which encouraged Indian industries such as textile mills and match factories
B1: it also led to national schools and colleges and spread the movement to other parts of India

long.q: State any four causes of the rise of the Assertive Nationalists.
scheme: B1: the Moderates' methods had failed to win significant reforms
B1: Curzon's policies, especially the Partition of Bengal, angered Indians
B1: famine and plague in 1896-97 and the harsh relief measures caused great suffering
B1: international events such as Japan's victory over Russia (1905) showed that an Asian nation could defeat a European power

long.q: Name the leaders known as Lal-Bal-Pal and state two methods of the Assertive Nationalists.
scheme: B1: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal
B1: they used boycott of foreign goods and swadeshi, and passive resistance
B1: they used national education and popular festivals (such as Ganapati and Shivaji festivals) to rouse the masses

long.q: State three objectives of the Home Rule Movement.
scheme: B1: to achieve self-government (home rule) for India within the British Empire
B1: to promote political education and discussion among the people
B1: to build confidence among Indians to oppose the government's repression and to win public support for Indian freedom during the war

questions.q: The All India Muslim League was founded in 1906 at:
questions.why: It was founded at Dacca on 30 December 1906, at a session of the Muhammadan Educational Conference, with Nawab Salimullah's support.

questions.q: The Simla Deputation of 1906 was led by:
questions.why: The Aga Khan led Muslim leaders to Lord Minto to ask for separate electorates.

questions.q: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced by:
o: the Government of India Act of 1858
questions.why: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 let Muslims elect their own representatives in separate constituencies.

questions.q: Who founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh?
questions.why: Sir Syed founded it in 1875 to spread modern education among Muslims; it later became Aligarh Muslim University.

questions.q: Which of these was one of the original objectives of the Muslim League?
o: To promote loyalty to the British government among Muslims
questions.why: Its early aims were loyalty to the British, protection of Muslims' political rights and avoiding hostility to other communities.

long.q: State any four factors that led to the formation of the Muslim League.
scheme: B1: the British policy of divide and rule, which encouraged Muslims to see their interests as separate
B1: the educational and economic backwardness of Muslims, who felt they could not compete with Hindus for jobs
B1: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's advice to Muslims to stay away from the Congress and remain loyal to the British
B1: the Partition of Bengal, which created a Muslim-majority province, and Muslims' fear of the Congress agitation against it

long.q: State the objectives of the Muslim League at the time of its founding.
scheme: B1: to promote among Muslims a feeling of loyalty to the British government
B1: to protect and advance the political rights and interests of Muslims and represent their needs to the government
B1: to prevent the rise of hostility among Muslims towards other communities

long.q: What was the Simla Deputation? What did it demand?
scheme: B1: it was a group of about 35 Muslim leaders, led by the Aga Khan, who met Lord Minto at Simla on 1 October 1906
B1: they demanded separate electorates, so that Muslims would elect Muslim representatives
B1: they also asked for representation in the councils and services greater than their numbers, considering their political importance

long.q: How did the British policy of divide and rule encourage communalism? Give two examples.
scheme: B1: after 1857 the British first distrusted Muslims, then, seeing the Congress grow, began to favour them to weaken the national movement
B1: example: the Partition of Bengal (1905) was presented as giving Muslims a province of their own
B1: example: separate electorates (1909) divided voters by religion

long.q: Why did the Congress agree to separate electorates in the Lucknow Pact of 1916? State one result.
scheme: B1: to win the League's cooperation and present joint demands for self-government to the British
B1: result: Hindu-Muslim unity grew for a time, but acceptance of separate electorates helped communal politics later

topics.name: Mahatma Gandhi and the National Movement

questions.q: Gandhiji's first satyagraha in India (1917) was on behalf of the indigo farmers of:
questions.why: In Champaran (Bihar) peasants were forced to grow indigo under the tinkathia system; Gandhiji's inquiry won them relief.

questions.q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was called off in 1922 because of the violence at:
questions.why: On 5 February 1922 a mob at Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur, UP) set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen, and Gandhiji withdrew the movement.

questions.q: The Dandi March of 1930 began the:
questions.why: Gandhiji walked from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi (12 March-6 April 1930) and broke the salt law there.

questions.q: The Quit India resolution was passed by the Congress on:
questions.why: It was passed at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942; Gandhiji gave the call ‘Do or Die’.

questions.q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919 took place in:
questions.why: General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful meeting protesting against the Rowlatt Act.

long.q: Explain the causes of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
scheme: B1: the Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed arrest and imprisonment without trial
B1: the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) and the government's failure to punish General Dyer
B1: the Khilafat issue: Indian Muslims were angered by the harsh treatment of the Sultan of Turkey (the Khalifa) after the First World War
B1: economic hardship after the war (rising prices, unemployment) and disappointment with the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms

long.q: State any four parts of the programme of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
scheme: B1: surrender of British titles and honours
B1: boycott of government schools, colleges, law courts and legislatures
B1: boycott of foreign cloth and use of khadi and swadeshi goods
B1: setting up national schools (such as Jamia Millia Islamia, Kashi Vidyapeeth) and panchayats to settle disputes

long.q: Why did Gandhiji choose salt for the Civil Disobedience Movement? State two features of the movement.
scheme: B1: salt was used by everyone, rich and poor, so the salt tax hurt all Indians and the issue could unite them
B1: making salt from sea water was a simple act anyone could do to break the law peacefully
B1: feature: people broke the salt law, boycotted foreign cloth and liquor shops, and refused to pay taxes
B1: feature: women took part in large numbers, and leaders such as Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan led it in the North-West Frontier

long.q: State three causes of the Quit India Movement.
scheme: B1: the failure of the Cripps Mission (March 1942), which offered only dominion status after the war
B1: the threat of a Japanese invasion: Indians felt they could defend India better if the British left
B1: rising prices, shortages and resentment against British rule during the war

long.q: Explain any two social ideals of Mahatma Gandhi.
scheme: B1: removal of untouchability: he called the untouchables Harijans (people of God) and worked for their entry into temples and wells
B1: Hindu-Muslim unity / uplift of women / swadeshi and village self-reliance through khadi and cottage industries / basic education (Nai Talim)

topics.name: The Forward Bloc and the Indian National Army

questions.q: Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Forward Bloc in:
questions.why: After resigning as Congress president in April 1939, he formed the Forward Bloc within the Congress in May 1939.

questions.q: Whom did Subhas Chandra Bose defeat in the election for Congress president at Tripuri (1939)?
questions.why: Sitaramayya was Gandhiji's candidate; Gandhiji said his defeat was his own, and Bose soon resigned.

questions.q: The Provisional Government of Free India (Azad Hind) was proclaimed at Singapore on:
questions.why: Bose proclaimed it on 21 October 1943; it was recognised by Japan, Germany and several other countries.

questions.q: The women's regiment of the INA was named after:
questions.why: The Rani of Jhansi Regiment was led by Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan (later Sahgal).

questions.q: Which slogan was given by Subhas Chandra Bose to the INA?
questions.why: ‘Dilli Chalo’ (On to Delhi) was his call to the INA; he also popularised ‘Jai Hind’.

long.q: State three objectives of the Forward Bloc.
scheme: B1: to rally all radical and anti-imperialist groups and fight for complete independence without compromise
B1: to organise peasants and workers and work for an agrarian revolution, ending landlordism
B1: to establish a socialist state after independence, with economic planning and industrialisation

long.q: Describe how the Indian National Army was formed and how Subhas Chandra Bose came to lead it.
scheme: B1: the idea of the INA was first carried out by Captain Mohan Singh, who formed it in 1942 from Indian prisoners of war captured by Japan in South-East Asia
B1: Rash Behari Bose, through the Indian Independence League, supported it among Indians living in South-East Asia
B1: after differences with the Japanese, the first INA broke up
B1: Subhas Chandra Bose reached Singapore in 1943 and took over command of the INA, reorganising it

long.q: State any three activities or achievements of the INA.
scheme: B1: it organised brigades named after national leaders (Gandhi, Nehru, Azad and Subhas Brigades) and a women's regiment
B1: Bose hoisted the Indian flag at Port Blair after Japan handed over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, renamed Shaheed and Swaraj
B1: INA troops advanced into India, hoisted the flag at Moirang in Manipur (April 1944) and took part in the Imphal-Kohima campaign

long.q: Give two reasons why the INA failed to achieve its aim.
scheme: B1: Japan's defeat in the war cut off the INA's supplies, weapons and air support
B1: heavy monsoon rains, disease and lack of food in the Imphal campaign / the death of Subhas Chandra Bose in an air crash (August 1945) left it leaderless

long.q: Explain the significance of the INA trials of 1945.
scheme: B1: three INA officers, Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, were tried for treason at the Red Fort
B1: they were defended by Bhulabhai Desai, Jawaharlal Nehru and others, and the trials roused nationwide protest, uniting Indians of all communities
B1: the trials, along with the naval mutiny of 1946, showed the British that they could no longer rely on Indian soldiers, which hastened independence

questions.q: The Cabinet Mission came to India in:
questions.why: The Mission of Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander arrived in March 1946.

questions.q: The Muslim League observed ‘Direct Action Day’ on:
questions.why: The League called for direct action to win Pakistan; it led to communal riots, first in Calcutta.

questions.q: The plan announced on 3 June 1947 for the partition of India is known as the:
questions.why: Lord Mountbatten's plan provided for two dominions, India and Pakistan.

questions.q: Which of these was a provision of the Indian Independence Act, 1947?
o: India would remain a colony until 1950
The office of the Secretary of State for India was abolished
Princely states had to join India
The Viceroy would rule both countries
questions.why: The Act created two dominions from 15 August 1947, ended the Secretary of State's office and let British paramountcy over the states lapse.

questions.q: Who was the first Indian Governor-General of independent India?
questions.why: Mountbatten was the first Governor-General of the Dominion of India; C. Rajagopalachari succeeded him in 1948.

long.q: State any four proposals of the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946).
scheme: B1: there would be a Union of India, including British provinces and princely states, dealing with defence, foreign affairs and communications
B1: the demand for a separate Pakistan was rejected
B1: provinces would be grouped into three sections (A, B and C), which could form their own constitutions
B1: a Constituent Assembly would be elected by the provincial assemblies, and an interim government of Indian leaders would be formed

long.q: State the main provisions of the Mountbatten Plan.
scheme: B1: India would be divided into two dominions, India and Pakistan
B1: the legislative assemblies of Punjab and Bengal would vote on whether to partition their provinces
B1: referendums would be held in the North-West Frontier Province and the Sylhet district of Assam
B1: a Boundary Commission would mark the boundaries, and the princely states would be free to join either dominion

long.q: Why did the Congress accept the partition of India? Give three reasons.
scheme: B1: widespread communal riots after Direct Action Day convinced leaders that partition was the only way to stop the bloodshed
B1: the Muslim League's obstruction in the Interim Government showed that the two parties could not work together
B1: the Congress wanted a quick transfer of power and a strong central government, which was not possible under the Cabinet Mission Plan

long.q: State any three provisions of the Indian Independence Act, 1947.
scheme: B1: two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, would be set up from 15 August 1947
B1: the Constituent Assembly of each dominion would have full power to make its constitution, and could act as its legislature
B1: British paramountcy over the princely states would lapse, and the post of Secretary of State for India would end

long.q: What was Direct Action Day? State one of its results.
scheme: B1: 16 August 1946, the day the Muslim League called for direct action to achieve Pakistan, after withdrawing its acceptance of the Cabinet Mission Plan
B1: it led to large-scale communal riots, first in Calcutta and then in Noakhali, Bihar and elsewhere

questions.q: Which countries formed the Triple Entente?
questions.why: The Triple Entente (completed 1907) faced the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy (1882).

questions.q: The heir to the Austrian throne was assassinated at Sarajevo on:
questions.why: Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife were shot by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist; this was the immediate cause of the war.

questions.q: The First World War ended with an armistice on:
questions.why: Germany signed the armistice on 11 November 1918; the Treaty of Versailles was signed later, on 28 June 1919.

questions.q: Which clause of the Treaty of Versailles held Germany responsible for the war?
questions.why: The war guilt clause (Article 231) made Germany accept blame, which was used to justify reparations.

questions.q: Which international body was set up after the First World War to keep peace?
questions.why: The League of Nations, based on Woodrow Wilson's ideas, began work in 1920 with its headquarters at Geneva.

long.q: Explain how the system of alliances was a cause of the First World War.
scheme: B1: Europe was divided into two armed camps: the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia)
B1: each group was suspicious of the other and prepared for war
B1: because of the alliances, a local quarrel between Austria and Serbia quickly drew in all the great powers

long.q: State four causes of the First World War other than the system of alliances.
scheme: B1: militant nationalism, which made each nation see its own interests as supreme
B1: imperialism: rivalry for colonies and markets, especially between Germany and Britain and France
B1: the arms race, including the naval race between Britain and Germany
B1: the Balkan problem and the immediate cause, the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo

long.q: Describe the events from the Sarajevo crisis to the outbreak of a general war in August 1914.
scheme: B1: on 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated at Sarajevo by a Serbian nationalist
B1: Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, sent Serbia an ultimatum and declared war on 28 July 1914
B1: Russia mobilised to support Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia and then France
B1: Germany invaded Belgium to reach France, and Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914

long.q: State any four terms of the Treaty of Versailles that affected Germany.
scheme: B1: Germany had to accept guilt for the war and pay heavy reparations
B1: Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France, and the coal mines of the Saar were given to France for 15 years
B1: the German army was limited to 100,000 men; Germany could have no air force or submarines, and the Rhineland was demilitarised
B1: Germany lost all its colonies, which became mandates, and lost land to Poland (the Polish Corridor), with Danzig made a free city

long.q: State three results of the First World War.
scheme: B1: four empires fell: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires
B1: new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia appeared on the map of Europe
B1: the League of Nations was set up; the harsh Treaty of Versailles left Germany bitter, which led to the Second World War

topics.name: Rise of Dictatorships: Fascism and Nazism

questions.q: Mussolini came to power in Italy after the:
questions.why: After the Fascist march on Rome in October 1922, the King invited Mussolini to become Prime Minister.

questions.q: Hitler became Chancellor of Germany in:
questions.why: President Hindenburg appointed him Chancellor on 30 January 1933; after Hindenburg's death in 1934 he became Führer.

questions.q: Which book did Hitler write while in prison?
questions.why: Mein Kampf (My Struggle), written after the failed 1923 putsch, set out his racial and nationalist ideas.

questions.q: Which country did Mussolini's Italy invade in 1935?
questions.why: The invasion of Abyssinia showed the League of Nations' weakness, as its sanctions failed.

questions.q: Which of these was a feature common to both Fascism and Nazism?
o: Rule by a single party and a single all-powerful leader
Belief in many parties and free elections
Support for the League of Nations
questions.why: Both glorified the state and the leader, banned opposition and relied on propaganda and force.

long.q: State four causes of the rise of Fascism in Italy.
scheme: B1: Italy was dissatisfied with the peace treaties: although on the winning side, it did not get the territories it expected
B1: economic crisis after the war: unemployment, inflation and strikes
B1: fear of communism among the middle class, landowners and industrialists, who backed Mussolini
B1: weak coalition governments and the appeal of Mussolini's strong leadership and nationalism

long.q: State four causes of the rise of Nazism in Germany.
scheme: B1: Germans resented the harsh and humiliating Treaty of Versailles
B1: the Weimar Republic was weak and unstable and was blamed for accepting the treaty
B1: the Great Depression (from 1929) caused mass unemployment and made people turn to extreme parties
B1: fear of communism, Hitler's oratory and Nazi propaganda, and anti-Jewish feeling that Hitler used

long.q: Explain any three features of Nazi ideology.
scheme: B1: extreme nationalism and the aim of uniting all Germans and winning ‘living space’ (Lebensraum) in the east
B1: racial theory: Germans were a superior ‘Aryan’ race, and Jews were blamed for Germany's problems and persecuted
B1: totalitarian rule: one party, one leader (the Führer), and the state controlling every part of life

long.q: State three steps Hitler took between 1933 and 1938 that broke the Treaty of Versailles or threatened peace.
scheme: B1: he withdrew Germany from the League of Nations (1933) and began rearming, bringing back conscription (1935)
B1: he sent troops into the demilitarised Rhineland (1936)
B1: he annexed Austria (Anschluss, 1938) and, after the Munich Pact, took the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia (1938)

long.q: State two ways in which Mussolini strengthened his rule in Italy.
scheme: B1: he banned other political parties and trade unions, and used his Black Shirts and secret police against opponents
B1: he controlled the press, schools and propaganda, and made peace with the Pope through the Lateran Treaty (1929)

questions.q: The Second World War began when Germany invaded:
questions.why: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

questions.q: The policy of giving in to Hitler's demands to avoid war is called:
questions.why: Britain and France followed appeasement, most famously at Munich in 1938.

questions.q: The USA entered the Second World War after Japan attacked:
questions.why: Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor (Hawaii) on 7 December 1941.

questions.q: On which date was the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima?
questions.why: Hiroshima was bombed on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945; Japan then surrendered.

questions.q: Which agreement of August 1939 made it safe for Hitler to attack Poland?
questions.why: Germany and the USSR agreed not to fight each other and secretly planned to divide Poland.

long.q: Explain how the policy of appeasement led to the Second World War.
scheme: B1: Britain and France allowed Hitler to break the Treaty of Versailles: rearming, reoccupying the Rhineland and annexing Austria
B1: at Munich (1938) they agreed to let Germany take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia, hoping he would be satisfied
B1: this made Hitler believe they would never fight, so he went on to occupy the rest of Czechoslovakia and then attack Poland

long.q: State four causes of the Second World War.
scheme: B1: the harsh Treaty of Versailles, which left Germany wanting revenge
B1: the failure of the League of Nations to stop aggression (Manchuria 1931, Abyssinia 1935)
B1: the rise of Fascism and Nazism and the forming of the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis
B1: the policy of appeasement, and the immediate cause: Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939

long.q: What was the immediate cause of the Second World War?
scheme: B1: Hitler demanded the free city of Danzig and a route through the Polish Corridor; Poland refused
B1: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France, who had guaranteed Poland's independence, declared war on 3 September

long.q: State any four important events of the Second World War, with the year of each.
scheme: B1: the fall of France (1940) and the Battle of Britain (1940)
B1: Germany's invasion of the USSR (Operation Barbarossa, 1941) and Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor (1941)
B1: the German defeat at Stalingrad (1942-43) and the Allied landings in Normandy (D-Day, 6 June 1944)
B1: Germany's surrender (May 1945) and the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki followed by Japan's surrender (August 1945)

long.q: State four consequences of the Second World War.
scheme: B1: enormous loss of life and property, including the Holocaust in which about six million Jews were killed
B1: the United Nations was set up in 1945 to maintain world peace
B1: the USA and the USSR emerged as superpowers, leading to the Cold War; Germany was divided
B1: colonial powers were weakened, which speeded up the independence of colonies in Asia and Africa, including India

questions.q: The United Nations came into existence on:
questions.why: The Charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945, now celebrated as UN Day.

questions.q: How many permanent members does the Security Council have?
questions.why: The USA, UK, France, Russia and China are permanent members with the power of veto.

questions.q: The International Court of Justice is located at:
questions.why: The ICJ, the UN's principal judicial organ, sits at The Hague in the Netherlands, with 15 judges.

questions.q: For how long is a non-permanent member of the Security Council elected?
questions.why: The General Assembly elects ten non-permanent members for two-year terms.

questions.q: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on:
questions.why: The General Assembly adopted it on 10 December 1948, now observed as Human Rights Day.

long.q: State any four objectives of the United Nations.
scheme: B1: to maintain international peace and security
B1: to develop friendly relations among nations based on equal rights and self-determination of peoples
B1: to achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems
B1: to promote respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all, and to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations

long.q: Describe the composition of the General Assembly and state three of its functions.
scheme: B1: all member countries are represented; each may send up to five representatives but has only one vote
B1: it discusses any matter within the scope of the Charter and makes recommendations
B1: it approves the UN budget and decides members' contributions
B1: it elects the non-permanent members of the Security Council and, on the Council's recommendation, admits new members and appoints the Secretary-General

long.q: Explain the veto power of the permanent members of the Security Council.
scheme: B1: decisions on important (substantive) matters need nine votes out of fifteen
B1: these nine must include the votes of all five permanent members
B1: so a negative vote by any one permanent member, called a veto, blocks the decision

long.q: Name the six principal organs of the United Nations.
scheme: B1: the General Assembly and the Security Council
B1: the Economic and Social Council and the Trusteeship Council
B1: the International Court of Justice and the Secretariat

long.q: State two functions of the Security Council in maintaining peace.
scheme: B1: it investigates disputes that may threaten peace and recommends ways of settling them peacefully
B1: it can take action against an aggressor, such as economic sanctions or the use of force through UN peacekeeping forces

topics.name: Major Agencies of the United Nations

questions.q: The headquarters of the World Health Organisation is at:
questions.why: WHO, set up on 7 April 1948 (World Health Day), is based at Geneva.

questions.q: UNESCO has its headquarters at:
questions.why: UNESCO works for education, science and culture from Paris.

questions.q: UNICEF was set up in 1946 mainly to:
o: help children in need, first in war-hit countries
questions.why: It began as the International Children's Emergency Fund for children after the Second World War; its work became permanent.

questions.q: Which UN agency prepares the list of World Heritage Sites?
questions.why: Under UNESCO's World Heritage Convention (1972), sites such as the Taj Mahal are protected.

questions.q: Which disease was declared eradicated from the world in 1980 after a WHO campaign?
questions.why: Smallpox was the first human disease eradicated; India was certified polio-free in 2014 but polio is not yet eradicated worldwide.

long.q: State any four functions of UNICEF.
scheme: B1: it provides food, medicines and shelter to children in emergencies such as war, floods and famine
B1: it supports immunisation of children against diseases such as polio, measles and diphtheria
B1: it works to improve child nutrition, safe drinking water and sanitation
B1: it promotes primary education, especially for girls, and the protection of children from abuse and child labour

long.q: State any four functions of the World Health Organisation.
scheme: B1: it works to control and eradicate diseases such as smallpox, polio, malaria and tuberculosis
B1: it helps countries improve their health services and train doctors and nurses
B1: it sets international standards for medicines, vaccines and food safety
B1: it gives information and guidance during epidemics and pandemics, and promotes research on health

long.q: State three functions of UNESCO.
scheme: B1: it works to spread education and remove illiteracy
B1: it encourages cooperation in science and research among nations
B1: it protects the world's cultural and natural heritage and promotes exchange of cultures

long.q: State two ways in which the work of UN agencies has benefited India.
scheme: B1: WHO and UNICEF helped India's immunisation drive, and India was certified polio-free in 2014
B1: UNESCO has listed many Indian monuments as World Heritage Sites and supports education and literacy programmes

long.q: What is meant by a specialised agency of the UN? Give two examples other than UNICEF.
scheme: B1: a specialised agency is an international organisation linked to the UN that works in one field, such as health, labour or education, coordinated through the Economic and Social Council
B1: WHO (World Health Organisation)
B1: UNESCO / ILO / FAO (any one)

questions.q: The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held in 1961 at:
questions.why: The first summit met at Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in September 1961 with 25 member countries.

questions.q: Panchsheel was first set out in an agreement of 1954 between India and:
questions.why: The five principles of peaceful co-existence appear in the 1954 India-China agreement on trade with Tibet.

questions.q: Which of these leaders was a founder of the Non-Aligned Movement?
questions.why: Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana) were its founders.

questions.q: Non-alignment meant:
o: remaining neutral in every dispute and staying silent
not joining either of the two power blocs led by the USA and the USSR
questions.why: Non-aligned countries kept an independent foreign policy and judged each issue on its merits.

questions.q: The Afro-Asian conference held in 1955, which prepared the ground for NAM, met at:
questions.why: The Bandung Conference in Indonesia brought newly independent Asian and African nations together.

long.q: State the five principles of Panchsheel.
scheme: B1: mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty
B1: mutual non-aggression
B1: mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs
B1: equality and mutual benefit
B1: peaceful co-existence

long.q: State four factors that led to the formation of the Non-Aligned Movement.
scheme: B1: the Cold War divided the world into two military blocs, and new nations did not want to be drawn into it
B1: newly independent countries wanted to protect their hard-won freedom and follow an independent foreign policy
B1: they needed economic help from both blocs for their development
B1: they wished to oppose colonialism and racism and to work for world peace and disarmament

long.q: State three objectives of the Non-Aligned Movement.
scheme: B1: to keep away from military alliances of the superpowers and reduce Cold War tension
B1: to oppose colonialism, imperialism and racial discrimination such as apartheid
B1: to promote world peace, disarmament and economic cooperation among developing countries

long.q: Explain India's role in the Non-Aligned Movement.
scheme: B1: Jawaharlal Nehru was one of its founders and shaped the idea of non-alignment
B1: India supported the freedom struggles of colonies and opposed apartheid in South Africa
B1: India hosted the seventh NAM summit at New Delhi in 1983, and has worked through NAM for disarmament and fairer world trade

long.q: Name any two founder leaders of the Non-Aligned Movement and their countries.
scheme: B1: Jawaharlal Nehru (India) / Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia)
B1: Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt) / Sukarno (Indonesia) / Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana)
